title: Where to Find Nginx and Apache Access Logs
content_md: On Debian and Ubuntu, Nginx logs to /var/log/nginx/access.log and error.log, and Apache to /var/log/apache2/access.log and error.log. On RHEL, Rocky and Alma, Apache uses /var/log/httpd/access_log and error_log, with underscores and no extension. In containers built from the official Nginx image, there are no log files at all: everything goes to stdout and stderr, so docker logs is your export. The web server log is often the first place an intrusion leaves a trace: the scanner sweeping for .env files, the exploit string, the POST to a file that shouldn’t exist. Prime Core has 812 detection rules for web server logs, mapped to 337 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: exploitation of public-facing apps (T1190), web shells (T1505.003) and vulnerability scanning (T1595.002). Get Started for Free Before you start Find the real paths. Virtual hosts often log somewhere custom. Ask the server itself: # Nginx: dump the full effective config and pick out the log directives sudo nginx -T 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'access_log|error_log' # Apache sudo apachectl -S sudo grep -Ri -E 'CustomLog|ErrorLog' /etc/apache2/ /etc/httpd/ 2>/dev/null On Debian-based Apache, virtual hosts without their own CustomLog end up in other_vhosts_access.log. People miss that one all the time. Check whose IP you’re logging. Behind a load balancer, CDN or reverse proxy, every request can appear to come from the proxy. That holds unless the server is set up to log the real client: set_real_ip_from and real_ip_heade
